headline_en: Baby Elephant Rescued from the River
summary_en: A deeply emotional and inspiring story has emerged from West Bengal's Jalpaiguri district. A three-to-four-day-old baby elephant was swept away here in the Teesta River. While crossing the river with its mother and the herd, it got separated in the strong current. Five fishermen fishing in the river near Malbazar saw it drowning. Without fear, these fishermen immediately turned their boat toward the baby elephant. They chased it by boat for three kilometers in the river's swift flow. After a lot of effort, the fishermen safely pulled the exhausted calf onto the boat. Inside the boat, the fishermen hugged the baby elephant to support it. Later, veterinary doctor Nick Doley thoroughly examined and cared for it. Forest department officials reunited the baby elephant with its mother. Everyone is wholeheartedly praising the courageous effort of the fishermen.

lead.title: The Elephant 'Hug' Went Viral. Here's What the Veterinarian Says It Really Meant
lead.summary: The Teesta was carrying the calf away. Near Spur Number 12, in the Malbazar subdivision of Jalpaiguri district in Bengal, a few fishermen noticed the tiny elephant being pulled along by the river's current. It was barely a few days old and had already been separated from its herd. The fishermen were out on the river when they saw it struggling in the water. They turned their boat towards the calf and followed it through the current for nearly three kilometres before they could reach it. By then, the calf had travelled several kilometres from where its herd had attempted to cross the Teesta. They pulled it into the boat. In the video that followed, the exhausted calf is seen being held close by the fishermen. For many people watching the footage, the image looked unmistakably like a hug. The moment has since travelled far beyond the river. Shared widely on social media, it has drawn praise for the fishermen who went after the calf and for the forest officials who helped reunite it with its mother. For a newborn elephant calf, the Teesta River became a terrifying journey away from his mother. Only 3–4 days old, he was swept nearly 5 km downstream by the river’s powerful currents while crossing with his mother. summary_en: Forty-year-old Alastair Cass was watching a match of his favorite football team, Arsenal, on TV. In the match, Arsenal suffered a heavy three-nil defeat against Brighton. Deeply frustrated by this loss, Alastair walked out of his house in anger. As soon as he stepped out, he suddenly heard the cries and screams of a woman. The woman was trapped chest-deep in mud and desperately needed help to save her life. Right after his team's defeat, Alastair stepped forward to save the woman's life and became a true hero for her.

headline_en: Homeless Students Get a Safe Home
summary_en: A wonderful initiative has been launched for college students in need. The Dax Program has opened a new hostel for students in Denver, USA. This organization provides housing for up to two years to students facing homelessness or financial hardship. This allows students to focus on completing their degrees without worrying about housing. This historic brick building in Denver has accommodation for fifteen students. The program is working in partnership with Metropolitan State University and Regis University. On this occasion, a student named Nikya Harrell shared her story. In the early days, Nikya had no roof over her head and was extremely distressed. With the help of the Dax Program, she found safe shelter, and her life improved. So far, this organization has provided shelter to nearly five hundred students across different cities.

lead.title: A Place to Sleep for Denver’s Homeless College Students
lead.summary: This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters. During her first semester at Chicago’s Malcolm X College, Nikya Harrell had had enough. It was winter, and she was cold. She was bouncing to and from family members’ houses and sometimes could only afford one meal a week. Harrell came to school overwhelmed and crying. A concerned friend suggested she see the school’s therapist, who connected her with the Dax Program, which offers students at risk of or experiencing homelessness a place to live for up to two years. Harrell came to Denver for Depaul USA’s Dax Program’s recent opening of the city’s first student residence near the Capitol building. Harrell had a message for other students who face challenges finding a place to live that she’s often repeated to herself: “You’re never alone.” Community members gather to bless the newly opened Depaul USA Dax Program housing on September 24, 2026, in Denver. Credit: Jason Gonzales / Chalkbeat Dax provides students with a safe living space that allows them to focus on getting a college degree without worrying about where they’ll sleep. The program has partnered with Metropolitan State University of Denver and Regis University, but wants to expand services to other local colleges and universities. The nonprofit provides resources to people experiencing homelessness and operates 11 Dax student housing programs in Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and New York. The program started in 2015 and has housed 494 students in those cities. The Denver Dax residence, an 1890s brick building that was originally a duplex in North Capitol Hill, is one of the national program’s larger residences and will be able to house up to 15 students. summary_en: In the world of architecture, a blind architect has done inspiring work. Chris Downey had been working as a normal architect for twenty years. In 2008, he lost his sight after a surgery. But Chris never lost heart in the face of this great challenge. He realized that paths and buildings could also be understood through sound. Chris began identifying directions from the echo of the wind chimes outside his home. After this, he incorporated elements of sound and touch into the design of buildings. He is no longer limited to just ramps or Braille. He has also helped design San Francisco's famous Salesforce Transit Center. His goal is to make public spaces accessible for blind and disabled people.

lead.title: How the Architecture of Sound Is Transforming Cities
lead.summary: B efore Chris Downey lost his sight, he had a wind chime on his front porch. After he became blind, he realized that he could listen out for it to help him find his way home. But after a few years, his nextdoor neighbor added a wind chime to their porch. And then the neighbor on the other side, just uphill, added a chime of their own. “Three in a row!” Downey said. He assumed at this point that his chime would no longer be able to help him locate his house. But then he noticed that the chime that the neighbor up the hill had hung was slightly higher in pitch compared to his own, and the neighbor who lived slightly downhill had hung lower, deeper chimes. “It was completely coincidental,” Downey said. “But they were perfectly sonified to match the topographic condition.” Downey had worked as an architect for 20 years before he became blind in 2008, and this chorus of wind chimes suggested a new direction in his work: The sounds of the city weren’t just decorative, musical — they could define the physical contours of a space as dramatically as a concrete wall or an open door to the street. Chris Downey played a significant role in the design of the Salesforce Transit Center in San Francisco. Credit: Engel Ching / Shutterstock He began developing a set of design principles that understood architectural accessibility not only in terms of wheelchair ramps and braille on elevator buttons, but ones that considered the ways that sound (and other senses) shaped the experience of blind and other disabled people navigating the built environment. He became part of an evolving conversation in inclusive design that expanded the idea of access, and reconsidered the place of the disabled body in public space. headline_en: 500 Lakes to Be Revived in Karnataka
summary_en: A major plan has been prepared to revive lakes in Karnataka. The state government has drawn up a 150-crore rupee plan to rejuvenate five hundred lakes across seven water-scarce districts. This project will be completed with assistance from the World Bank. These five hundred lakes include sixty-eight in Bengaluru Rural, sixty-seven in Bengaluru Urban, ninety in Chikkaballapur, ninety-six in Tumakuru, eighty-six in Kolar, forty-nine in Kalaburagi, and forty-four in Bidar. Under this project, silt will be removed from the lakes, embankments will be raised and strengthened, canals will be repaired, and beautification will be carried out. According to the World Bank, this network could help manage floods and droughts.

lead.title: Karnataka Plans to Revive 500 Lakes: What Does a Truly Healthy Lake Look Like?
lead.summary: For a city built around lakes, Bengaluru has spent years trying to answer: how do you bring a lake back? The answer usually lies with the physical things that are easiest to see: remove the silt, repair the bund, clear the weeds, fix the feeder channel, and make the edges accessible. Now, Karnataka is preparing to do this at scale. The state has drawn up a Rs 150-crore plan to rejuvenate 500 lakes across seven water-stressed districts, PTI reported on 22 September 2026. Of these, 135 are in Bengaluru Urban and Bengaluru Rural.   The proposed works include desilting, strengthening and raising bunds, repairing canals and feeder channels, and beautification. The project is planned with World Bank assistance. The 500 lakes are spread across Bengaluru Rural (68), Bengaluru Urban (67), Bidar (44), Chikkaballapur (90), Kalaburagi (49), Tumakuru (96) and Kolar (86). But Bengaluru’s experience with its restored lakes suggests that bringing back water is only one part of bringing back a lake . So, what should a healthy urban lake actually look like? There are at least three tests. The first test: What enters the lake? Stand beside a Bengaluru lake, and the first thing to ask is: what is flowing into it? Historically, Bengaluru’s lakes formed a connected cascade. Water moved from one tank to another across the city’s natural terrain. The World Bank’s 2025 technical assessment of the Karnataka Water Security and Resilience Programme describes the remaining lake network as having the potential to help the city manage both floods and droughts. But that function depends on the quality and quantity of water entering the system. headline_hi: दुर्लभ सेबों को बचाने की मुहिम
summary_en: Dave Benscoter is a retired FBI agent. For more than twenty years, he has been searching for century-old apple trees to save them from extinction. An incident related to this unique work took place in the year 2012. At that time, Dave was pruning trees in the backyard of a friend's house. While working there, he found an apple he had never seen before. Ever since, he has been continuously working to discover and preserve such century-old trees.

headline_hi: एआई पर भारी बुज़ुर्गों का अनुभव
summary_en: According to a new survey conducted in the UK, more than seven out of ten people believe that AI chatbots can never replace the advice of elders. The study of two thousand adults found that twenty-one percent of people use these artificial intelligence tools for help several times a week. Despite this, ninety-two percent of people believe that certain forms of wisdom and knowledge can only be gained through life experience. Seventy-one percent of participants in the study feel that AI can never take the place of lessons taught by elders.
